title: A meta-analysis of the long-term effects of antihypertensive therapy on the risk of major cardiovascular disease across 51 randomized trials
authors: Yang Q, Bidel Z, Canoy D, Zeng G, Cushman WC, Rodgers A, et al.
population: Participants of 51 randomised trials of blood-pressure-lowering treatment held in the Blood Pressure Lowering Treatment Trialists' Collaboration, excluding those with heart failure at baseline; mean age about 65 years, mean baseline blood pressure about 152/87 mm Hg
funder: British Heart Foundation (FS/19/36/34346). The funder had no role in study design, data collection and analysis, decision to publish or preparation of the manuscript. The acknowledgements add: this study used data from a trial supported by Boehringer Ingelheim; Boehringer Ingelheim had no role in the design, analysis or interpretation of the results; however, they were allowed to review the paper for medical and scientific accuracy regarding Boehringer Ingelheim substances and for intellectual property considerations. That pre-publication review is an industry role in publication, so the class is industry.

result: Annual incidence of major adverse cardiovascular events was highest in the first year, 3.0% with treatment against 3.6% in controls. Standardised to a 5 mm Hg lower systolic blood pressure, the hazard ratio for major adverse cardiovascular events was 0.88 (95% CI 0.84 to 0.91) in year 1, 0.88 (0.85 to 0.92) in years 1 to 2, 0.94 (0.90 to 0.98) in years 2 to 3, 0.87 (0.83 to 0.92) in years 3 to 4, 0.97 (0.91 to 1.03) in years 4 to 5 and 0.94 (0.87 to 1.01) after 5 years (p for trend 0.006), so relative benefits appeared early and did not compound. Cumulative absolute risk reduction for major adverse cardiovascular events rose from 0.30% (0.20 to 0.40) at 1 year, a number needed to treat of 337, to 1.25% (0.94 to 1.57) at 5 years, a number needed to treat of 80; for stroke it rose from 0.07% (0.02 to 0.12) to 0.52% (0.36 to 0.68), numbers needed to treat 1535 and 192. In an individual-participant network meta-analysis of 34 trials across angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors, angiotensin II receptor blockers, beta blockers, calcium channel blockers and thiazide diuretics, no class showed compounding benefit for major adverse cardiovascular events (all p for trend above 0.05); heart failure prevention diminished over time with calcium channel blockers (p for trend 0.010) and with thiazide diuretics, whose first-year hazard ratio was 0.40 (0.30 to 0.54, p for trend 0.034).
